1	# Investigation notes: issue #230, a web control surface on the remote port
2	
3	Read: CLAUDE.md, docs/lessons.md (general architecture lessons only; nothing
4	about the remote port), docs/remote-client.md §4.1-4.4 and §5, §9, and the code
5	below. Line numbers are as in this worktree (branch
6	dispatch/230-a-web-control-surface-the-remote-port-se, HEAD 7fe8949).
7	I did not read docs/design.md's remote status section (starts at
8	`## Remote client (2026-10-12)`, line 3107, through 3584) beyond locating it, and
9	did not read the Swift code beyond the invite parser.
10	
11	## On-disk record and rehydration (before the pane)
12	
13	Nothing new is needed on disk for the page itself; the page is code in the
14	binary, not data.
15	
16	- A browser is a `PairedDevice` (`src/ports/remote.rs:96`: id, name, scope,
17	  `token_sha256`, created, `last_seen`), persisted in `<data dir>/devices.json`
18	  through `RemoteFiles::save_devices` (`src/adapters/remote.rs:83`), atomic
19	  write. The token is never stored, only its SHA-256 (`token_sha256`, line 345).
20	  Nothing in the struct says what kind of client it is; the name is the only
21	  label. A user-agent-derived name fits the existing field with no schema bump.
22	- Rehydration of "paired" is the existing path: `StoreLoaded`/identity and
23	  devices load at start, the bearer hash is looked up by
24	  `AppCore::device_by_token` (`src/core/remote.rs:145`). A cookie carrying the
25	  same token would hash to the same record, so revocation
26	  (`AppAction::RevokeDevice`, handled in `app.rs:486`, which also drops the
27	  device's subscriber queues and so closes its socket) works unchanged.
28	- Key rotation deletes devices (§5 of the spec), so a browser's stored token
29	  stops working; the page needs a distinct "identity changed / revoked" reading
30	  of a 401 vs a changed `/info` key (the server answers 401 `unauthorized`
31	  with no distinction between revoked and never paired:
32	  `authenticate`, `src/app.rs` ~3130-3150).
33	- Client-side state (token if it is kept in `localStorage`, the pinned key) is
34	  per-browser, outside the data dir, and cannot be rehydrated by the host. With
35	  an `HttpOnly` cookie the token is not even visible to the page. A cookie's
36	  lifetime (session cookie vs `Max-Age`) decides whether a browser restart
37	  loses the pairing; the host holds the device record either way.
38	- The pairing window is `PairingWindow` in core (`src/core/remote.rs`), never
39	  saved (the spec says it is like `ENV_SETUP_WINDOW`).
40	- Waiting/live state on the page is not stored; it is the existing read model
41	  (`/waiting`, `/projects/{id}/sessions`, events with `revision`), refetched on
42	  `changed`. Nothing to rehydrate beyond reconnect + `hello` + snapshot (§4.4
43	  "Subscribe first, then snapshot").
44	
45	## Code the issue touches
46	
47	### Serving paths: `src/app.rs`
48	- `serve_remote` `src/app.rs:3017-3127`. Line 3023: `request.path.strip_prefix("/api/v1/")`
49	  else 404 `not_found` via `refuse(..., false)`. This is where `GET /` and
50	  static paths would branch first. `/info` and `/pair` are matched at
51	  3028-3033 before `authenticate`.
52	- `authenticate` ~3131: only reads `request.bearer`. No cookie input exists.
53	- `remote_info` `app.rs:3568-3603`: returns server_id, server_name, protocol,
54	  capabilities, `spki_sha256`, version, limits, `pairing_open`. Caveat: the page
55	  compares the URL's `key` to the `/info` key *over the same connection it then
56	  posts to*; `/info` is served by whoever answers, so it proves consistency, not
57	  authenticity (the issue already notes this).
58	- `remote_pair` `app.rs:3606-3665`: checks `spki_sha256` field equals the
59	  host's, then the code (case-insensitive), counts `PairingFailed` on either
60	  failure, names the device from the `device_name` body field (empty becomes
61	  "Device"), returns JSON `{token, scope, server_id, device_id}` through
62	  `envelope`. No headers can be set today (see below).
63	- `remote_subscribe` `app.rs:2723`: requires `request.upgrade`, authenticated
64	  by the same bearer path; registers a `Subscriber {device, all}`.
65	- `refuse` ~3754 and `remote_reply` ~3695 shape errors.
66	- The remote port is only bound on non-loopback after pairing is required;
67	  `advertise_remote` (3002) / `remote_addr` (3014).
68	
69	### The HTTP adapter: `src/adapters/remote.rs`
70	- `RemoteRequest` `:360-385`: method, path (query split off), query pairs
71	  (undecoded, "ids and numbers only"), body, `bearer`, `upgrade`. Headers are
72	  dropped after `read_request` (`:444-517`); it reads only
73	  `content-length`, `authorization`, `upgrade`, `sec-websocket-key`.
74	  Not read: `cookie`, `origin`, `host`, `user-agent`, `sec-websocket-protocol`,
75	  `if-none-match`. Query values are not percent-decoded.
76	- `RemoteReply` `:389`: `{status, body: Vec<u8>, authenticated}`. No headers,
77	  no content type.
78	- `respond` `:530-552`: hardcodes `Content-Type: application/json`,
79	  `Content-Length`, `Connection: keep-alive`; no `Cache-Control`, no CSP, no
80	  `Set-Cookie`, no `X-Content-Type-Options`. Status reasons cover 200, 400, 401,
81	  403, 404, 405, 413, 429, 503, 504 only (no 304).
82	- `respond_upgrade` `:519-527`: 101 reply with `Sec-WebSocket-Accept` only; no
83	  `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo (a browser that offered subprotocols fails the
84	  handshake if the server does not echo one of them).
85	- No `Origin` check anywhere on the upgrade (matters once a cookie
86	  authenticates: cross-site WebSocket hijack).
87	- Pools `:567-568`: `MAX_UNAUTHENTICATED = 4`, `MAX_PAIRED = 12`. The accept
88	  loop (`:700-730`) counts *every* new connection against the unauthenticated
89	  pool, and moves it to the paired pool only on the first reply with
90	  `authenticated: true` (`connection`, `:770-875`). A page load before pairing
91	  (HTML + CSS + JS + `/info` + `/pair`, over however many parallel keep-alive
92	  connections the browser opens) all sit in the 4. Timeouts: 5 s handshake and
93	  first request line (`HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT`), 30 s idle (`IDLE_TIMEOUT`).
94	- Rate windows `:583-640`: `Limits::limited` matches exactly `PAIR_PATH`
95	  (6/min) and `INFO_PATH` (60/min); any other path returns false (unlimited).
96	  A static path would be unrate-limited by default.
97	- `connection` hands every request to the frame over `INBOX` (64), drained
98	  `DRAIN_PER_PASS` (8) per pass; static files would go through the frame
99	  unless short-circuited on the connection thread (a design choice).
100	- TLS: `make_identity` `:95-127` builds the certificate with
101	  `CertificateParams::new(Vec::new())`: no subject alternative names, CN
102	  `Switchboard <server_id>` only; validity is rcgen's default (not examined).
103	  `tls_config` `:144-157` sets no ALPN, so browsers will speak HTTP/1.1 (fine
104	  for the hand-rolled reader). The client pin `pinned_client` `:168` ignores
105	  names; browsers will not.
106	- `local_address` `:962`: the host's LAN IP via a UDP connect trick; the
107	  address is an IP literal. An IP-literal URL and a certificate with no IP SAN
108	  is the case a browser rejects as a name mismatch.
109	
110	### The pairing window: `src/ui/remote.rs`
111	- `pairing` `:141-227`; payload built `:156-166` as JSON `{server_id,
112	  spki_sha256, code, addresses: ["ip:port"]}`; `qr_texture` `:280` encodes the
113	  payload; `Copy invite` button `:203-208` copies the JSON; the dialog text
114	  says "Scan, or type the key and the code" (`:194`). `short_hash` `:303`,
115	  `spaced` `:314`. The address is `ip:port` with the port from
116	  `cx.remote_port` else `identity.listen.port`.
117	- Scope is chosen in `draft.scope` (`:213-224`), radio Read-only/Control.
118	- Devices list/Revoke is `devices` `:230`; the dialog does not yet say anything
119	  about browsers.
120	- Core: `src/core/remote.rs` (`remote_action` `:21`, `pairing_at` `:152`,
121	  `new_device` `:166`).
122	- Script aids: `src/script.rs:729-737` (`pairing <code>|close`,
123	  `remote-devices`), README dev-aid list at README.md ~277-278 says the QR text
124	  is on the clipboard for `switchboard-remote pair "$(pbpaste)"`.
125	
126	### Native text-pairing path that must keep working
127	- `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:94-117`: `PairingInvite`
128	  is `Decodable` JSON with `server_id`, `spki_sha256`, `code`, `addresses`;
129	  `parse` is `Wire.decode(PairingInvite.self, from: text)`. A URL would need
130	  `parse` to accept `https://addr/?code=&key=&id=` (the `key` and `id` query
131	  names differ from the JSON names).
132	- `client/Sources/switchboard-remote/main.swift:12-13, 105-125`: the CLI takes
133	  the JSON as one argument or `<host:port> <code> <spki_sha256>`.
134	- visionOS paste field: `client/Sources/SwitchboardUI/BrowserView.swift:792,
135	  849, 883`; `ConnectionManager.pair(invite:)`
136	  `client/Sources/SwitchboardClientCore/ConnectionManager.swift:482`.
137	- Swift tests/fixtures: `client/Tests/*`, `client/Fixtures` (rewritten by
138	  `SWITCHBOARD_WRITE_FIXTURES=1`, `tests/remote.rs:1587 write_fixtures`).
139	
140	### Tests today: `tests/remote.rs`
141	- Helper `http` `:245-297` is a raw TLS client with a pinned config; it sets
142	  only `Authorization` and `Content-Length`, parses only `Content-Length`
143	  from response headers (returns status + body, not headers), so asserting
144	  `Content-Type`/CSP/`Cache-Control` needs a helper that returns headers.
145	  `call`/`get` `:299-331`, `pair` helper `:406`.
146	- Relevant existing tests: `info_is_served_to_anyone_and_every_other_read_is_refused_unpaired`
147	  `:426`; `the_allowlist_refuses_everything_else_with_no_side_effect` `:682`
148	  (asserts `/api/v2/projects` is 404 `not_found`; a `GET /` test belongs
149	  beside it); `a_pairing_with_another_hosts_key_or_the_wrong_code_counts_and_three_close_the_window`
150	  `:582`; `pair_is_rate_limited_per_listener` `:1406`; stalled strangers filling
151	  only their pool (listed in README); revoke `:658`.
152	- No `web/` directory exists. The only embedded assets in the tree are
153	  `include_bytes!` fonts/icon (`src/ui/theme.rs:203-211`, `src/main.rs:167`);
154	  `include_str!` is not used anywhere yet.
155	
156	### Spec and docs to amend
157	- docs/remote-client.md: §4.1 bounds (line ~126-134, the pool/rate bullets),
158	  §4.3 endpoints table (line ~159) which says everything else is refused,
159	  §5 (line ~302-320) pairing: QR JSON text, "bearer header over the pinned
160	  connection, never in a URL", "Require pairing before anything but `/info`
161	  and `/pair`", and the "Loopback-only without auth" line; §9 (no relay).
162	- docs/design.md "Remote client (2026-10-12)" status section (3107-3584).
163	- README.md Layout table (line ~383 `src/adapters/remote.rs`, ~423
164	  `src/ui/remote.rs`, ~437 `tests/remote.rs`), the dev-aid note at ~277; a new
165	  `web/` dir needs a Layout line. CHANGELOG.md Unreleased line (user-visible).
166	- CLAUDE.md rules that bind the plan: `src/core` stays deterministic; no new
167	  dependency for the page; secrets never in a URL/log (the invite URL carries
168	  the one-time code, and the issue's own plan removes it from the address bar);
169	  never name a client/customer in tests or fixtures; no tool attribution in
170	  commits/PR bodies; schema bump only if a serialized model type changes (a
171	  device kind field would; a name-only record would not).
172	
173	## Facts the tree settles that bear on the issue's decisions
174	- A cookie cannot be set or read today: no response-header channel exists
175	  (`RemoteReply` and `respond` above) and `Cookie` is not parsed. Either choice in
176	  decision 2 changes `RemoteReply`/`respond`/`read_request` (and a
177	  `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` echo in `respond_upgrade` if the subprotocol route is
178	  chosen).
179	- The frame decides `authenticated: true` in `RemoteReply`; the connection
180	  thread uses it to move a connection between pools, so a cookie-authenticated
181	  request would need the same mapping.
182	- A `GET /` that isn't under `/api/v1/` is currently a 404 JSON `not_found`
183	  produced at `app.rs:3023` after a frame round-trip; the `Limits::limited`
184	  and pools sit below that in the adapter.
185	- `/pair`'s wrong-key and wrong-code paths both count toward the window's three
186	  failures; a page that compares keys first avoids sending the code to a
187	  mismatched host, but the rejection is also server-enforced.
188	- The device name arrives only from the `/pair` body (`device_name`); the User-
189	  Agent is not read by the host, so "Safari on iPhone" is derived either in the
190	  page script from `navigator.userAgent` or in `read_request` by adding a
191	  header read.
192	- The QR is currently a JSON payload with an address list; a URL carries one
193	  address, and the address is chosen once by `local_address()`.
194	
195	## Not checked
196	- The Swift test files and `docs/design.md` remote status contents in detail.
197	- Whether `qrcode` crate handling of a longer URL payload changes QR size/version
198	  (the URL carries a 64-hex key, a UUID, an 8-char code, an address: roughly
199	  150 characters vs the current JSON of similar length).
200	- The exact certificate validity rcgen sets by default, and whether anything in
201	  `Cargo.toml` pins the `rcgen` version/features for SANs or dates.
202	- How `ControlSocket`-style `serve` handles `last-response` for non-Claude
203	  sessions on the wire (the page needs the screen for those); `session` view
204	  fields the card excerpt uses were not enumerated.
205

214	- [source] The browser: after the user accepts a certificate warning, does Safari on iOS remember the exception for the IP and port across tabs, `fetch` and `new WebSocket("wss://...")`, and for how long (it is known to drop the exception on some page reloads)?

# Spikes

Throwaway crates and scripts that answered the Spike 0 questions in
`docs/design.md` before any product code was written. Each directory has a
README with the commands run, their output, and a recommendation. They are
kept for reference and are not built by the main crate.

| Dir | Question | Answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `01-claude-resume` | Can Claude Code sessions be captured and resumed? | Yes: `--session-id <uuid>` at launch, `--resume <uuid>` later from any terminal. Transcripts pruned after 30 days unless `cleanupPeriodDays` is raised. |
| `02-process-host` | tmux or own PTYs? | tmux on a private server: sessions outlive the app, reattach works, ~3 ms round trip. PTY adapter kept as fallback and for tests. |
| `03-session-state` | How to know "waiting on you"? | Claude Code hooks (`PermissionRequest`, `Stop`, `SessionEnd`) via a tiny `switchboard-hook` binary and a Unix socket; OSC 777 text from the raw stream as the hook-free fallback. |
| `05-keychain` | Can secrets live in the Keychain without prompts? | Yes for a bundle signed with a stable identity and identifier: the item ACL is `identifier + certificate`, so rebuilds read silently. Ad-hoc builds prompt per rebuild. |
| `06-pane-size` | Why is the embedded pane wider than the widget? | `window-size manual` ignored the client; `latest` makes the window follow whichever client attached last. Re-applied on launch for servers that outlive the app. |
| `07-clone-session` | Can a session be cloned up to a chosen message? | Yes: copy the transcript prefix before the chosen prompt, substitute a fresh UUID for `sessionId`, save it `0600` beside the original; `--resume <new>` opens the truncated history and the original is untouched. |
| `08-promptbox-embed` | Can Prompt Box be the agent message box? | Yes: same egui 0.36, drawn into a bottom panel unchanged, a `Clipboard` adapter turns Send into a hand-off; needs an embedded mode, a sink port, and focus-scoped shortcuts in promptbox. |
| `09-popout` | Can a session live in a window of its own? | Yes: an immediate viewport drawn from the main frame holds the page, terminal, and side panel; its frame is saved to settings and restored. |
| `10-nunchuk-serial` | Can a nunchuk drive the working set over USB serial? | Yes: one line per button change or stick flick from the Feather, read on a thread that reconnects; round trip 2 to 9 ms. Firmware in `firmware/nunchuk`. |
| `11-gate-sandbox` | Can Dispatch's pipeline commands be confined to the ticket's tree on macOS? | Yes: `sandbox-exec` with `(allow default)`, writes denied except the tree, the attempt directory, the lane's caches and a base set; ~5 ms start-up; a refused write is `EPERM` and a tagged `deny(1)` line in the unified log. `setuid` programs and keychain creation fail inside it. |
| `12-hidden-frames` | Does the frame loop keep running while the window is occluded or minimized? | Not before the fix: with the app hidden, a control query timed out after 10 s and was answered at once on unhide. With the tick and `pump` in `App::logic`, hidden queries answer in 75 to 103 ms (eframe's 100 ms throttle for invisible windows). The sleep and wake cycle is not yet measured. |
| `13-dispatch-service` | Can a Dispatch service be a Switchboard service session, and how is its port read? | Yes: `$SHELL -lc 'exec "$@"' dispatch-service env PORT=<port> npm start` finds `npm`, answers (CRA in 27 s), and is gone with its port 200 ms after `kill-session`. A port is free only if `0.0.0.0`, `127.0.0.1` and `[::1]` all bind: CRA listens on `*`, which a loopback bind does not see. |
| `14-env-exec` | Do a pane's record id and launch token reach a child, so `switchboard-env exec` can resolve its sets? | Yes for a shell grandchild of a tmux pane started with `-e`; the binary's path is covered by `tests/control.rs`. The `aws-vault` form and the no-prompt run under Dispatch's launch flags were not run and are left to the owner. |
| `15-paste-buffer` | Can a multi-line send be bracketed only for a pane that asked for it? | Yes: `load-buffer -` then `paste-buffer -p -r -d` frames the text in `ESC[200~` .. `ESC[201~` for a pane with `bracket_paste_flag` 1 and delivers it bare otherwise; `-r` keeps LF, `-d` leaves no buffer. CR passes through and tmux 3.7c shows ESC as a literal `^[`, so the sender turns CR into LF and removes ESC. `send-keys -H` passes the markers to every pane. Measured on tmux 3.7c. |
| `16-base-pipeline` | Can Dispatch find a merged pull request's merge commit and read the base's pipeline on it? | GitHub, yes: `mergeCommit` on `gh pr list` and `gh pr view`, and the commit's `check-runs` (a short hash works) show the base's run in progress and then finished. Bitbucket's reads were not run (the token could not be read in the run); the adapter follows the documented `merge_commit.hash`, commit `statuses` and pipeline `steps`, with a read by number when a list row lacks the commit; until they are run, a wait on a Bitbucket base pipeline is refused. |
| `18-tmux-argv` | Do `new-session -e` values show in a process listing, and can they reach tmux another way? | Yes, they did: the server keeps the argv of the client that started it. `tmux start-server \; source-file -` with the `new-session` line on stdin keeps every value and the pane command off any argv; cold and warm both work, errors still return, and double-quoted values with `\n` for line breaks round-trip (single quotes lose a line starting with `#`). Measured on tmux 3.7c. |
| `19-structured-ask` | Does a card's answer to a structured ask reach interactive Claude Code as the next user message, sent once, both at the prompt and when held until the turn's `Stop`? | Yes: `Owner answered "<question>": <answer>`, typed as one line, arrived as its own user message once in both cases; a held answer went out only after the `Stop`. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.293 by the ignored gate test `a_structured_answer_arrives_as_the_next_prompt`. |
| `21-evidence-writes` | Which writes reach a stage's evidence directory, outside the agent's cwd, without a prompt? | The Write tool, under the attempt directory's `Edit(//<dir>/**)` rule. Bash `cp`, `mv` and `mkdir` ask, and `--add-dir` does not change that. A Playwright MCP screenshot is refused outside the server's roots unless it runs with `--allow-unrestricted-file-access`. Measured on Claude Code 2.1.295 and `@playwright/mcp@0.0.82`. |
| `22-remote-port` | Can a pinned-TLS HTTP and WebSocket port run on std with every request answered by the frame thread, and what does it cost? | Yes: `rustls` + `rcgen` + `tungstenite` + `mdns-sd`, no Tokio; the frame's share is under 0.25 ms per pass, latency is one frame interval, the pools and the subscriber overflow hold under a stall and an unread socket, Bonjour is seen by `dns-sd`. A 146 MB transcript parses in 290 ms at 575 MB peak, so content work leaves the frame thread. ctime and inode see the file changes mtime and size miss. |
| `04-terminal-view` | Embedded terminal or hand-off? | Hand off agents to Ghostty (`open -na Ghostty --args ... -e cmd`, raise by title); embed `egui_term` for shells, commands, services. |

Findings are folded into `docs/design.md` under "Spike 0 results".

# MCP Server Instructions

The following MCP servers have provided instructions for how to use their tools and resources:

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>\n\n<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>\n\n<?claude block s1?>\n\n<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

entries.name: WebFetch
entries.description:
Fetches a URL, converts the page to markdown, and answers `prompt` against it using a small fast model.

- Fails on authenticated/private URLs — use an authenticated MCP tool or `gh` for those instead. claude.ai artifact links (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}) are published artifacts: read them with the Artifact tool (action "read"), not WebFetch or curl.
- Fails on localhost and other hostnames without a dot; for a local server, use curl via Bash.
- HTTP is upgraded to HTTPS. Cross-host redirects are returned to you rather than followed; call again with the redirect URL.
- Responses are cached for 15 minutes per URL.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from

prompt.description: The prompt to run on the fetched content

offset.description: Character position in the page text to start reading from. Use it to read on through a page too long for one call, with the value the previous result gave.

entries.name: WebSearch
entries.description:
Search the web. Returns result blocks with titles and URLs. US-only.

- The current month is (provided in the conversation below) — use this when searching for recent information.
- `allowed_domains` / `blocked_domains` filter results.
- After answering from results, end with a "Sources:" list of the URLs you used as markdown links.

allowed_domains.description: Only include search results from these domains

blocked_domains.description: Never include search results from these domains

mode.description: "standard": the normal web search: quick and cheap; right for straightforward lookups (reference facts, official pages, documentation, well-known people, places and topics) and simple follow-up lookups. "extended": a thorough, fresh search at several times the cost and latency.

The results point to one cause: Chrome stopped checking the Common Name (CN) field, so a self-signed certificate for an IP address needs the IP in a Subject Alternative Name (SAN) field.

- **Why the error appears:** Chrome 58 and later ignore the CN and look only at the SAN. One forum reply says the error means the address you typed doesn't match a name or IP on the certificate. Starting with version 58 of Chrome, Chrome doesn't look to the Common Name field of a certificate, it looks only to the subjectAlternativeName field.
- **Fix:** Regenerate the certificate with the IP in the SAN. One thread describes the same fix for a firewall reached by IP. Use either FQDN or IP address. Another source gives the same advice, saying the certificate should be re-generated to include a Subject Alternative Name extension, or to enable an option in Chrome to allow them.
- **Example config:** A Graylog user tried adding an alt_names section to the OpenSSL config with subjectAltName= @alt_names and an IP entry. That is the general approach, but the thread doesn't confirm it worked for them.
- **Workaround:** Chrome's "Advanced" then "Proceed (unsafe)" option gets past the warning for a single session. One user reported the exception rule [ADVANCED -> Proceed to … (unsafe)].

Sources: community.graylog.org, community.nethserver.org, community.atlassian.com, forum.netgate.com, truenas.com community, kb.metricinsights.com. These are mostly forum posts and a vendor knowledge base, not Chrome's official documentation, and I did not verify the OpenSSL steps.

The search turned up several reports and a long-running WebKit bug that match your problem. Accepting the certificate for the HTTPS page doesn't carry over to `wss://` on iOS Safari.

- **Core issue:** Safari's handling of WebSocket connections differs from its handling of HTTPS. A reported case on an iOS device had the certificate installed as a profile, yet the secure socket still closed with an "invalid certificate chain" error (OSStatus -9807) while the https address was not treated as secure by the system.
- **Bug history:** WebKit Bug 41419 has been open since 2010. Its reporter found that Safari did not trust the self-signed certificate, and setting it to always trust made the WebSocket connection work. A mailing-list thread describes the same pattern: after the user accepts the warning, wss connections still fail in Safari and WebKit, whereas Chrome honors the acceptance for both protocols.
- **Subject Alternative Name:** A ThinLinc bug report found that on iOS 13 Subject Alternate Name is the critical missing piece. Adding that makes things work. Certificates were also expected to set Extended Key Usage and keep validity periods short.
- **Recent iOS versions:** A developer forum thread reports that on iOS 26 beta, a secure connection fails even though the certificate has been accepted and the page loads as https, with a "certificate for this server is invalid" error.

**Practical takeaways:** Make sure the certificate's SAN includes the exact hostname or IP the WebSocket uses, add Extended Key Usage, and keep the validity period short. Install and trust the certificate as a profile, and test with the hostname or IP that the page uses. If the problem persists, the iOS version and the certificate's SAN and EKU fields are the first things to check. I found no official Apple fix in these results.

Links: [{"title":"rfc6455 websocket checklist","url":"https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/@shuji-bonji/rfcxml-mcp/blob/83092edb94a262a4fd63c5daabe5fb35de920066/examples/rfc6455-websocket-checklist.md"},{"title":"github.com","url":"https://github.com/gobwas/ws/issues/81"},{"title":"[Bug 23576] New: Clarify what to do when received null value subprotocol in reply to non-empty subprotocol","url":"https://lists.w3.org/Archives/Public/public-webapps/2013OctDec/0229.html"},{"title":"show bug","url":"https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=23576"},{"title":"greenbytes.de","url":"https://greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.pdf"},{"title":"oneuptime.com","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-24-websocket-protocol-error/view"},{"title":"www2.greenbytes.de","url":"https://www2.greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.pdf"},{"title":"conference.greenbytes.de","url":"https://conference.greenbytes.de/tech/specs/rfc6455.pdf"},{"title":"Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF)                          I. Fette","url":"https://ietf.org/rfc/rfc6455"}]

The search turned up one clear rule and one gap, but I did not reach the RFC's full text, so the omission case is only supported by secondary sources.

- **Unrequested subprotocol: fail.** RFC 6455 says that if the server's response names a subprotocol the client did not offer, the client must fail the connection. The RFC's text covers a response that includes Sec-WebSocket-Protocol with a subprotocol absent from the client's handshake, and requires the client to fail the connection.

- **Omitted subprotocol: not explicitly required to fail.** A W3C bug report (Bug 23576) argues that RFC 6455 requires failure when the server answers with a subprotocol the client did not request, but not when the client requested subprotocols and the server returns none. It adds that RFC 6455 itself doesn't require a client to abort connection establishment in that case. The bug's author suggested clarifying the spec, which implies the question was open at the time. That is a 2013 discussion, not normative text, so check the current RFC and any errata before relying on it.

- **Practical implication.** A client that wants to require a subprotocol must check the response itself and close the connection if the header is missing. A server-side library issue shows the same gap: a server-side check on the subprotocol was never invoked when the client sent no Sec-WebSocket-Protocol header, so the connection was accepted. That is a server-side symptom, not the client rule.

The search turned up a few likely causes, though none of the sources is an official Apple or Google document.

**Safari rejects Secure cookies on non-secure pages.** A WebKit Bugzilla thread (bug 232088) says Secure cookies are not accepted from non-secure pages. Commenters there note that this is notably different to every other browser where localhost is treated as a secure context. Safari still treats localhost as secure in other checks, such as `window.isSecureContext`, which makes the behavior confusing. A Descope troubleshooting page reports the same pattern for HTTP pages, saying Safari will store the cookie only when executed in HTTPS page context.

**Self-signed certificates trigger warnings, and Safari is stricter about exceptions.** A SecuritySpy forum user reported that Safari showed "This Connection Is Not Private" for a self-signed certificate, even after proceeding and entering admin credentials. Another user noted that Chrome or Firefox on my mac as they seem to allow you to add a permanent exception. The same thread points out that the warning can also appear when the address in the URL differs from the one in the certificate. That matters if you connect by IP address and the certificate was issued for a hostname.

**Possible fixes:**
- Use HTTPS for the page that sets the cookie, so the Secure attribute is accepted. A locally trusted certificate avoids the warning entirely.
- Make sure the certificate covers the exact IP address or hostname you use.
- For local development only, drop the Secure attribute. An AI-generated forum answer suggests this, but it is not documented by Apple, and it sends cookies unencrypted, so don't use it in production.

Overall, the cookie problem and the certificate warning appear to be two separate issues. Safari's rule against Secure cookies on HTTP pages is the more likely cause of the missing cookie, and the self-signed certificate is a separate source of friction.

The spec says the response "indicates the use of a subprotocol that was not present in the client's handshake," and then the client "MUST _Fail the WebSocket Connection_."

If the response omits `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol`, the spec doesn't treat that as a failure. The Subprotocol In Use is "the null value if that header field was not present in the server's handshake."

The document doesn't mention user certificate exceptions or overrides, so it says nothing about whether a user can accept an unverified certificate.

- **The problem:** Developers on Apple's forums reported that the iPadOS Safari user agent matched macOS Catalina's, which made server-side OS detection unreliable. Since on iPadOS User Agent in Safari is same as on MacOS Catalina, what is recommened way to distinguish OS on server side?

- **Caveats:** An Apple forum commenter said the approach seems this is not the best way to handle this. A third-party user-agent guide advises against relying on OS tokens for critical logic and recommends validating on real devices. Also, the reported values come from 2019–2022 posts, so check them on current iPadOS and macOS versions before relying on them.

The search turned up a few real-world reports matching this behavior, but no authoritative explanation of why it happens in QR-scanner or in-app-browser contexts specifically.

- **Proxmox (2024):** Proxmox used `SameSite=Strict` on its UI cookies, and the cookie was not sent on the initial page load when users followed a link to a Proxmox URL from elsewhere. The UI then treated the user as logged out and cleared the cookie. The MDN reference says that setting it to 'lax' is similar to 'strict', but sends the cookie when navigating *to* our origin even from other sites, so they switched to Lax, and the patch was applied by the maintainer on October 15, 2024. The same thread notes that one Firefox ESR build also dropped the cookie on subsequent requests, which the author was unsure was the same issue.
- **Mozilla Support forum:** A user reported that the same steps were performed on different browsers (Samsung Browser, Firefox on windows) but all of them sent the cookies. The reported failure was on Android, after opening a link from inside another app, and it blocked a follow-up `window.reload`. The question was still open in the search results, with no confirmed root cause.
- **Reference definitions:** Strict is documented as cookies are only sent in same-site requests, meaning no cookies are transmitted in cross-origin requests, including those triggered by a user clicking a link from another site. Lax is documented as sent with same-site requests and top-level navigations (e.g., when a user clicks a link from another site).

**Takeaway:** A Strict cookie is withheld on a cross-site top-level navigation, which includes a link opened from a QR scanner or another app. Switching to `SameSite=Lax` is the usual fix when the cookie must survive that first load. The search did not confirm how each QR scanner or in-app browser classifies the navigation's site, so test on the specific clients you care about.

**Short answer:** The page doesn't quote the CSP3 spec text, so it can't confirm the exact matching rule. It does indicate that `connect-src 'self'` was meant to allow same-host, same-port WebSocket connections, and that Safari added support in Safari 16.0.

**Spec intent (per the thread):**
- Klings proposed allowing `ws(s):` requests to the same host/port under `'self'`. Mikewest committed a change in October 2015, and Klings said it "should do the trick for same host/port web sockets."
- The issue was reopened in February 2018 because annevk said "It seems this wasn't fixed properly yet."
- Whether `ws:` on an `http:` page matches `'self'` (raised by amacneil in 2015) isn't clearly resolved in the thread.

**Browser implementations:**
- **Chrome:** Fixed in 71.0.3559.6 (Dev), around September 2018, per skyzyx's comment.
- **Firefox:** Fixed by September 2018 (Dev and Stable). A later report says Firefox 120.0b9 regressed, while 119.0.1 worked.
- **Edge:** Edge 17 (EdgeHTML) already supported it when the WPT test was written. Chromium-based Edge inherited that support.
- **Safari:** WebKit fixed it in r292266, shipped in Safari Technology Preview 144 (May 2022), and it reached **Safari 16.0** (September 2022). Earlier reports were on Safari 12.1.1 and 12.1.2, and Safari 13 was still affected.
- **Opera:** Not tested in the WPT suite. The commenter assumed it inherited the Chromium fix.

The search didn't turn up a definitive explanation for why Safari forgets the exception on reload, but a few results are relevant.

- **Closest match:** A SecuritySpy user on Safari 12 reported that after clicking through the warning, Safari asked for admin credentials and then showed the same warning again. Safari is complaining that the SSL certificate is invalid - this will be either because it is self-signed (by default, SS generates you a self-signed certificate), or because you are connecting to the server using a different address that is set in the certificate. So the address mismatch is a likely cause, not just the self-signed status.
- **How the bypass works:** A Vultr guide says Safari shows a dialog and then asks for Touch ID or your password to change certificate trust settings. If you want to revoke the certificate, launch Keychain Access and delete the certificate in the login keychain.
- **Durable fix:** Apple's developer forums advise against overriding server trust in code, and suggest if you can avoid doing so, you should. Installing the certificate on the device as trusted is the cleaner route. A Jamf admin reported trying to download and upload the cert into the config profile. The result of that attempt isn't in the snippet.
- **Other checks:** Glendale's guide suggests checking that the device date and time are correct, and noting that if you are using a VPN service, that may also cause this problem.

Given the lack of a direct answer, a useful next step would be to search for the Keychain trust settings for a self-signed IP certificate on iOS, or for whether Safari keys exceptions to the exact hostname. Also worth checking whether the certificate's subject alternative names include the IP address being used.

Links: [{"title":"Referrer policy configuration","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Practical_implementation_guides/Referrer_policy"},{"title":"Referrer-Policy header","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy"},{"title":"Referrer-Policy header","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Security-Policy/referrer"},{"title":"referrer policy","url":"https://http.dev/referrer-policy"},{"title":"HTMLLinkElement: referrerPolicy property","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/HTMLLinkElement/referrerPolicy"},{"title":"what are the different types of referrer policies","url":"https://docs.piano.io/en/analytics/what-are-the-different-types-of-referrer-policies"},{"title":"HTMLAreaElement: referrerPolicy property","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/HTMLAreaElement/referrerPolicy"},{"title":"HTTP headers | Referrer-Policy","url":"https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/?p=433231"},{"title":"HTMLAnchorElement: referrerPolicy property","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLAnchorElement/referrerpolicy"},{"title":"HTMLScriptElement: referrerPolicy property","url":"https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTMLScriptElement/referrerPolicy"}]

The search results cover each directive and confirm that `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` is the default, with one outlier source to discount.

**Directives, from most to least strict (per MDN):** no-referrer: Never send the Referer header. same-origin: Send the Referrer header, but only on same-origin requests. Under `same-origin`, cross-origin requests carry no referrer at all, so the policy does not reveal the full URL to other sites.

**The default:** MDN describes `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` as the policy that applies when none is specified, or when the supplied value is invalid. Previously the default was no-referrer-when-downgrade. Under this policy, same-origin requests keep the full URL including the query string, while cross-origin requests get only the origin. Requests that downgrade from HTTPS to HTTP send no referrer. (Sources: the origin, path, and query string for same-origin requests; the origin only for cross-origin requests at the same security level; and no Referer header to less secure destinations.)

**Query string exposure:** This matters for your question. Any policy that sends the full URL, such as `unsafe-url` or the same-origin case of `strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, can expose query parameters. Under `unsafe-url`, MDN warns that this policy will leak potentially-private information from HTTPS resource URLs to insecure origins. Under `no-referrer` and `same-origin`, query strings never reach cross-origin destinations.

**Browser caveat:** MDN notes that in recent versions of Firefox and Safari, "unsafe" directives (no-referrer-when-downgrade, origin-when-cross-origin, and unsafe-url) behave like strict-origin-when-cross-origin.

**Conflicting source:** The Piano Analytics page says the default is `no-referrer-when-downgrade`. That matches the pre-2020 spec but not current browsers, so I would not rely on it for the default behavior.

(WebKit Bug 41419)","url":"https://lists.webkit.org/pipermail/webkit-dev/2011-June/017386.html"},{"title":"Websocket Error Chrome, I suspect that there may be a more su","url":"https://vm-3863995b.na4u.ru/zity/websocket-error-chrome.html"},{"title":"Websocket network error: The certificate is self-signed, and untrusted","url":"https://forum.qt.io/post/41192"},{"title":"Chromium Code Reviews","url":"https://codereview.chromium.org/304093003"},{"title":"show bug","url":"https://bugzilla.mozilla.org/show_bug.cgi?id=1187666"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://bugs.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419"},{"title":"oneuptime.com","url":"https://oneuptime.com/blog/post/2026-01-24-websocket-ssl-handshake-errors/view"},{"title":"Is Websocket Secure (wss) supported?","url":"https://forums.creativeclouddeveloper.com/t/is-websocket-secure-wss-supported/2422"},{"title":"WebKit Bugzilla","url":"https://www2.webkit.org/show_bug.cgi?id=41419"}]

The search didn't turn up a Chromium document that states this behavior directly, but the related sources point to the same answer: a certificate exception accepted on an HTTPS page generally doesn't carry over to WebSocket connections.

- **Browsers don't share the exception by design, at least in WebKit.** A WebKit bug (41419) proposed silently accepting a certificate the user had already approved for an HTTPS page when connecting to a WebSocket on the same domain and port. The thread shows the maintainers were skeptical of letting users make that call. "We don't want users to make the decision whether an invalid certificate means that they are unsafe."
- **The WebSocket spec requires failure.** The spec says that if the TLS handshake fails, such as when the certificate can't be verified, the WebSocket connection fails. If /secure/ is true, perform a TLS handshake over the connection. If this fails (e.g. the server's certificate could not be verified), then fail the WebSocket connection and abort these steps.
- **Chromium reportedly declined the feature.** A forum post says a related Chromium issue (146848) was closed as WONTFIX. That's secondhand, so verify it before relying on it.
- **Firefox users hit the same wall.** A Mozilla bug (1187666) about self-signed WSS was also closed as WONTFIX. Commenters described the workaround as visiting the HTTPS endpoint directly and adding an exception, which is the same workaround you're describing. The user shouldn't have to go to the port directly first to add the exception.
- **Errors look generic.** One source notes that Chrome will often report a close code 1006 if there is an error during the HTTP Upgrade to Websocket, so a certificate failure may show up only as a generic WebSocket error.

Based on the sources, the pattern you're seeing is probably a per-origin exception that the WebSocket stack doesn't honor, not a bug in your server. The reliable fixes are a trusted certificate (for example, mkcert for local development) or a certificate whose hostname matches the one the client uses. I didn't find a primary Chromium source confirming the exact per-origin behavior, so treat that part as my inference.

content.content:
**Status:** The bug is closed as RESOLVED WONTFIX. Mozilla's Patrick McManus said Firefox doesn't show a dialog for failed subresources, and that a `wss://` connection counts as one. He said `wss://` requires certificate validation, and a stored exception is the accepted route.

**Does a user-accepted exception apply to wss on the same host:port?** Yes. The reporter found that after adding the exception at `https://localhost:8080`, the websocket connected. Another commenter confirmed the same behavior for `wss://1.2.3.4:9000`.

**Workaround:** Open the HTTPS URL for the websocket's host and port directly in the browser (for example, `https://localhost:8080/`), accept the self-signed certificate, then load the page that opens the websocket. The reporter noted that this is a workaround, not a fix, since the browser never prompts for the exception from the page that needs it.

The search turned up consistent evidence that `navigator.userAgentData` is Chromium-only as of the latest data.

- **Safari:** caniuse lists Safari, including Safari on iOS, as not supporting the API in every released version through 27, with only the Technology Preview listed as "support unknown" (3.1 through 26.3, 26.4, and 26.5 to 27 are all unsupported, and the Technology Preview is unknown). The iOS entries are unsupported too (3.2 through 26.5).
- **Firefox:** also unsupported in every version listed (2 through 151, with later versions also unsupported).
- **Chromium browsers:** Chrome and Edge support it from roughly version 90 onward, and Opera from about 76. Chrome for Android and Samsung Internet also support it.
- **Secure context:** caniuse's secure-context variant shows the same Safari and Firefox gaps, so the API needs HTTPS in practice. MDN also flags the feature as not Baseline because it does not work in some of the most widely-used browsers.
- **Workaround:** a Mozilla webcompat shim shows the pattern for non-Chromium fallbacks. It checks whether the API exists and, if not, derives a platform guess from the user-agent string and `navigator.platform` (source: Firefox webcompat injection, bug 1898952).

Practical takeaway: wrap any `navigator.userAgentData` access in a feature check and fall back to `navigator.userAgent` or, preferably, feature detection. Caniuse's data here appears to be a snapshot, so check the live page before relying on exact version numbers.

content.content:
The page says Chrome is removing support for matching domain names against a certificate's `commonName`, and it treats `subjectAltName` (SAN) as the correct field.

- **Fallback removed:** RFC 2818 uses SAN names and falls back to `commonName` only when no SAN is present. The page says that fallback has been deprecated since 2000 but is still supported by some TLS clients.
- **Why it's ambiguous:** The page says "the commonName is ambiguous," and that this has caused security bugs. SAN fields, by contrast, make it clear whether a certificate is meant for an IP address or a domain name.
- **SAN required:** The page says the CA/Browser Forum baseline requirements have "required the presence of a subjectAltName since 2012." Firefox has required SAN for newly issued publicly trusted certificates since version 48.
- **Impact:** The page considers the compatibility risk low. Enterprises that need `commonName` matching for internal certificates can use the `EnableCommonNameFallbackForLocalAnchors` policy.

The page doesn't describe how IP addresses are matched beyond noting that SAN fields make the IP-versus-domain distinction unambiguous.

# Facts for issue #230 (web control surface)

No spike was run: the questions the plan turns on (a real Safari/Chrome on a real LAN with this host's certificate) need a device and a person's tap, so they go to the owner. `git status` is clean.

## Settled

### The tree
- `last-response` for a non-Claude session is refused `400 no_conversation` ("only a Claude Code session has a conversation"); a Claude session with no resume handle yet gets `400 no_conversation` ("has not started a conversation yet"). The page falls back to `screen` on that code. Evidence: `src/app.rs:1869-1886`.
- `SessionView` carries `kind`, `liveness`, `card` (the card's word), `waiting`, `waiting_reason`, `name`, `last_activity_ms`, `pending`. It has no one-line excerpt field; the card's excerpt is not on the wire. The page uses `card`/`waiting_reason`, or a `last-response` read. Evidence: `control/src/lib.rs:637-690`.
- `/api/v1/waiting` is its own collection, and `?scope=all` lists Dispatch worker sessions. Ordering waiting-first is the host's rank (`docs/remote-client.md:169, 388`); the page needs `sessions` for kind/name, since `waiting` is a membership list. Evidence: `docs/remote-client.md:169,239,388`.
- Swift tests assert `PairingInvite.parse` only on the JSON form (`testInviteParsesTheQRText`); `parse` is a plain `Decodable` decode, so a URL form needs a branch before the decode and the JSON test stays untouched. Evidence: `client/Tests/SwitchboardProtocolTests/FixturesTests.swift:157-165`, `client/Sources/SwitchboardProtocol/Info.swift:94-117`.
- The certificate has no SAN: `CertificateParams::new(Vec::new())` plus a CN; rcgen 0.14.10 default validity is 1975-01-01 to 4096-01-01. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:101-107`; `~/.cargo/registry/src/*/rcgen-0.14.10/src/certificate.rs:84-85`.
- The SPKI hash depends on the key alone (`key.subject_public_key_info()`), so a certificate re-issued with an IP SAN over the same key keeps `spki_sha256` and the pins. Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:113`.
- With `local_address()` = `None` there is no address to put in a URL (it returns `None` with no network). Evidence: `src/adapters/remote.rs:958-970`.
- Pool, rate and header facts are as the investigation lists them (every new connection counts in the 4-slot unauthenticated pool until a reply is `authenticated: true`; only `/pair` and `/info` are rate-limited; `respond` hardcodes JSON; no cookie/Origin/User-Agent read). Evidence: investigation notes, `src/adapters/remote.rs:444-552, 567-640`.

### The world
- **Chrome ignores the Common Name; a certificate for an IP needs an IP SAN.** Chrome 58 removed CN matching (opt-out only by enterprise policy `EnableCommonNameFallbackForLocalAnchors`). Searching found many reports of `ERR_CERT_COMMON_NAME_INVALID` for exactly this case, with "Advanced > Proceed (unsafe)" the workaround users report. Evidence: https://developer.chrome.com/blog/chrome-58-deprecations ; forum reports from the search (graylog, nethserver, netgate, truenas) are leads that agree.
